name: Blacklight-reactive hair dye

card.summary: A fluorescent vivid hair colour that glows under blacklight, such as the lights used in nightclubs, giving a striking colour effect.
card.aka: UV hair dye; glow-in-the-dark hair dye
card.note: Allergy and irritation risks of hair dyes generally apply; no product-specific safety data was reviewed.

quick.overview:
Blacklight-reactive hair dyes are a newer category of alternative or vivid hair colour that fluoresce under blacklights, such as those often used at nightclubs. Wikipedia lists them among the alternative colour options that produce shades not found in nature.

The appearance payoff is a standout hair colour that looks bright in daylight and glows under UV light. No clinical trials on these specific products were found.
quick.how: Vivid dyes of this type generally contain tint only and no developer, so they show their brightest colour mainly on light blond hair; darker hair usually needs bleaching first. Semi-permanent versions typically last about 4 to 8 shampoos, though blue and purple can persist for months on pre-lightened hair.
quick.risks: Hair dyes in general can cause allergic reactions and skin irritation with redness, itching or burning, sometimes appearing hours later, and semi-permanent dyes may still contain p-phenylenediamine or related colourants. Pre-lightening hair adds its own chemical stress. Manufacturers often recommend a patch test; European dermatologists have debated this advice.

lead: Blacklight-reactive hair dyes are alternative or vivid hair colours that fluoresce under blacklights, such as those often used at nightclubs.[1] They belong to the category of colours not found in nature, such as green and fuchsia, which Wikipedia notes contain only tint and no developer, so they show their bright colour mainly on light blond hair, with darker hair usually needing bleaching first.[1]

For people who want to stand out visually at events, the draw is a hair colour that changes appearance under UV lighting. Product-specific research on fluorescence, longevity or safety is not found in standard references; general information on hair dye effects applies.

chain: Apply fluorescent vivid dye (often to pre-lightened hair)
Colour shows bright in daylight and glows under blacklight
Distinctive hair appearance at clubs and events
angle.text: The dye changes hair colour directly, and the blacklight-reactive type adds a glow effect under UV lighting such as nightclub lighting.

paras: Wikipedia's hair colouring article describes blacklight-reactive dyes as a more recent addition to vivid colour products that fluoresce under blacklights, such as those often used at nightclubs.[1] Vivid colours of this kind generally contain tint only and no developer, so gold, yellow or orange undertones in hair that has not been lightened enough can muddy pinks, blues and greens.[1]

Semi-permanent dyes sit under the outer cuticle layer rather than lightening hair, and their colour typically lasts about 4 to 8 shampoos.[1] Blue and purple shades on bleached or pre-lightened hair can take several months to wash out.[1]

Hair dye can cause allergic reactions and irritation, with redness, itching, burning and sores that may appear hours or a day later.[1] Semi-permanent dyes may still contain p-phenylenediamine or related colourants, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer considers some hair dyes potentially mutagenic and carcinogenic, although the Wikipedia article notes that evidence linking hair dye to cancer in humans is limited and inconsistent.[1] Manufacturers often recommend a 48-hour patch test, and European dermatologists have advised against it, arguing it can increase sensitisation risk.[1]
